<reason>Both sides were strong, but B built the cleaner path. A's externality framing and curb-space argument were genuinely powerful, and A's closing ("size is not a proxy—it is the cost") was the best reframe of the debate. But A never repaired the Turn 3 misdescription of insurance (liability coverage does price third-party pedestrian injury), which B punished precisely; A's Pressure Questions cited nonexistent reference IDs; and A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped. B held one consistent master-frame—does a static size tier track harm better than use-scaled tools?—answered both pressure questions with direct A1/A2 distinctions, and closed by granting A's best premise and showing the tiered motion still doesn't scale per foot or per pound, plus the velocity-squared gap. A kept a live curb-space route and B somewhat overread the motion as mandating cliffs and overstated A's "retreat" to revenue, so the margin stays slim, but B landed more unrepaired, decisive damage and made the decision easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's two-stage judo: the Turn 4 correction that liability insurance already prices third-party pedestrian risk (never repaired by A), capped by the closing move granting "size is the cost" and then showing the motion charges a category tier, not per foot or per pound—turning A's strongest line into an instrument critique.</best_rebuttal>
